early_history_summary: Jobim began studying piano at age 14 on an instrument given to his sister by his stepfather, who sent him to classically trained teachers. name: Steve Howe
milestone_by_age_26: Joined Yes in March 1970 at age 22 and recorded landmark progressive rock albums The Yes Album (1971), Fragile (1971), and Close to the Edge (1972) by age 25, establishing himself as one of the genre's defining guitarists.
early_history_summary: Howe grew up in Holloway, North London, and received his first guitar at age 12 in 1959. He left school at 15 after failing his O-levels and began playing in London bands from 1964, including the Syndicats, Tomorrow (whose 1967 single 'My White Bicycle' became a psychedelic classic), and Bodast. He also did session work at EMI before joining Yes in 1970.
primary_leverage_engine: Technical depth on guitar across multiple styles
family_context_summary: Grew up in a middle-class family apartment in Holloway, North London. His father was head chef at a Bishopsgate restaurant. Parents bought him his first guitar at age 12.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a chef; no music domain background in family. Parents' record collection exposed him to Les Paul and Tennessee Ernie Ford.
primary_early_advantage_tags: London 1960s music scene, session work, band experience from teens
evidence_summary: Howe grew up in a middle-class London family with no music background but was immersed in the 1960s London rock scene from his teens. He taught himself guitar from 12, left school at 15, and spent six years playing in bands and doing EMI session work before joining Yes at 22. His distinctive multi-style guitar approach was honed through years of practical performance before his breakthrough. The prog rock wave of the early 1970s amplified his skills into major commercial and critical success.

name: Antoni Tàpies
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded the avant-garde magazine Dau al Set in 1948 at age 24 and exhibited at the I Saló d'Octubre in Barcelona; held his first solo exhibition at Galeries Laietanes in 1950 at age 26.
early_history_summary: Tàpies grew up in a cultured Catalan republican household in Barcelona and began drawing self-taught during the Spanish Civil War. A serious lung disease at 17 led to two years of convalescence during which he intensified his artistic practice, reading widely and copying Van Gogh and Picasso. He briefly studied law before devoting himself to painting, leasing a studio in 1946 and connecting with Catalan avant-garde figures by 1947-48.
primary_leverage_engine: Catalan avant-garde network and self-taught material experimentation
family_context_summary: Born to Josep Tàpies Mestres, a lawyer and Catalan nationalist who served with the Republican government, and Maria Puig Guerra. His father's friendship with leading Catalan public figures exposed Tàpies to a rich cultural and political environment from childhood.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a lawyer connected to Catalan republican intellectual circles; maternal grandfather was civically and politically active. Family provided cultural environment but not specifically art-world access.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Catalan avant-garde network, Dau al Set co-founders, convalescence as catalyst, Barcelona cultural milieu
evidence_summary: Tàpies grew up in a cultured Catalan republican family in Barcelona, exposed to leading cultural figures through his father's connections. A serious lung disease at 17 catalyzed his artistic dedication during two years of convalescence. By 1947-48 he had connected with the Catalan avant-garde (Joan Prats, J.V. Foix, Joan Brossa) and co-founded Dau al Set magazine, providing both a creative platform and exhibition opportunities. His first solo show at 26 marked his entry into the professional art world.

name: Luigi Riva
milestone_by_age_26: Helped Cagliari achieve promotion to Serie A in 1964 at age 19; by 26 he was a European champion (1968), Serie A top scorer, and had led Cagliari to the 1969-70 Scudetto at age 25.
early_history_summary: Born into poverty in Leggiuno, Lombardy, Riva lost his father to a factory accident at age 9 and was sent to a religious boarding school. He began playing amateur football for Laveno Mombello as a teenager, scoring 63 goals in two seasons, then joined Legnano in 1962. Cagliari signed him in 1963 for 37 million lire, and he immediately helped the club reach Serie A for the first time.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical talent — powerful left foot and aerial ability
family_context_summary: Born into a poor family in Leggiuno. Father Ugo worked multiple jobs (hairdresser, tailor, factory worker) and died in a work-related accident when Luigi was 9. Mother Edis worked as a maid and died soon after. Riva was sent to a strict religious boarding school and later worked in a lift factory.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family connection to professional football. Extreme poverty and orphanhood marked his early life.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Exceptional left foot, speed and strength, orphaned young, football as escape, Italian football pipeline
evidence_summary: Riva overcame extreme poverty and orphanhood to become one of Italy's greatest strikers. His exceptional physical talent — a powerful left foot, speed, and aerial ability — was evident from his amateur teens. Signed by Cagliari at 18, he helped them reach Serie A at 19 and became the league's dominant scorer, winning Euro 1968 at 23 and the Scudetto at 25. His adversity (orphaned at 9, boarding school, factory work) created the urgency that drove his football career as an escape path.

family_context_summary: Born in Ried im Innkreis, Upper Austria. Family valued science; a high school teacher in Hietzing, Vienna inspired him and five of 22 classmates to study physics.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond family valuing science.

name: Elvis Presley
milestone_by_age_26: Recorded 'That's All Right' at Sun Records in July 1954 at age 19, widely regarded as the beginning of rock and roll; became an international sensation by 1956 at age 21 with 'Heartbreak Hotel' and multiple chart-topping hits.
early_history_summary: Presley grew up in a working-class family in Tupelo, Mississippi and later Memphis, Tennessee. He made a demo acetate at Sun Studio in 1953 for $4, and was called back by Sam Phillips in 1954. His improvised recording of 'That's All Right' with guitarist Scotty Moore and bassist Bill Black launched his career. His Sun contract was sold to RCA in late 1955 for $35,000, and 'Heartbreak Hotel' became his first million-selling single in early 1956.
primary_leverage_engine: Unique vocal style and musical synthesis across racial lines
family_context_summary: Born to Vernon and Gladys Presley in a two-room house in Tupelo, Mississippi. The family was working-class and moved to Memphis in 1948 where Vernon worked various jobs. No financial resources or music industry connections.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in music or entertainment. Father worked various manual and factory jobs.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Memphis/Sun Records, Beale Street, Sam Phillips mentorship, rock and roll wave, working-class background
evidence_summary: Presley came from a poor working-class family with no music connections but grew up in Memphis, the epicenter of the emerging rock and roll movement. His natural vocal talent and charismatic style, combined with Sam Phillips's mentorship at Sun Records and the explosive cultural wave of rock and roll, propelled him from unknown truck driver to international sensation by age 21. The convergence of Memphis's music-rich environment (Beale Street, gospel churches, country and R&B traditions) with his unique ability to synthesize across racial musical lines was the key early advantage.

name: Abdus Salam
milestone_by_age_26: Awarded the Smith's Prize at Cambridge in 1950 at age 24 for the most outstanding pre-doctoral contribution to physics; his PhD thesis on quantum electrodynamics earned him an international reputation and an invitation to the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton in 1951 at age 25.
early_history_summary: Salam was a prodigy from Jhang, British India, scoring the highest marks ever recorded in the Punjab University Matriculation Examination at age 14. He published his first scientific paper at 17, earned his MA in mathematics at 20, and won a scholarship to St John's College, Cambridge, where he completed a double First in mathematics and physics in two years instead of three. His PhD thesis contained fundamental work in QED that gained him international recognition before age 26.
primary_leverage_engine: Exceptional mathematical ability and Cambridge physics ecosystem
family_context_summary: Born in Jhang, a small town in British India (now Pakistan). His father was an official in the Department of Education in a poor farming district. The family had a long tradition of piety and learning but limited financial means.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an education official who valued academic achievement; family had tradition of piety and learning. No direct physics or science domain background, but strong educational emphasis.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cambridge scholarship, Smith's Prize, prodigy, QED thesis, Punjab education system, IAS Princeton invitation
evidence_summary: Salam was a clear prodigy from a modest family in rural Pakistan, scoring record examination marks at 14 and publishing a scientific paper at 17. His father's role in education provided a culture of academic achievement. A scholarship to Cambridge gave him access to the world's leading physics ecosystem, where his exceptional mathematical ability led to a double First, the Smith's Prize, and a PhD thesis that earned international recognition — all by age 25. The elite institutional pipeline from Punjab to Cambridge to Princeton was the dominant early advantage structure.

evidence_summary: Montagnier grew up in wartime France with an amateur scientist father who inspired his interest. name: José Saramago
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Saramago published his first novel 'Terra do Pecado' in 1947 at age 25, but it had no material impact and he abandoned literary writing for 19 years afterward. His real literary career began in his 50s with 'Baltasar and Blimunda' (1982) and the Nobel Prize came in 1998. The first novel publication was not a material milestone.
early_history_summary: Saramago was born to landless peasants in Azinhaga, Portugal. His family moved to Lisbon where he attended a technical school and trained as a mechanic. He worked various jobs — mechanic, administrative clerk — while reading voraciously at the public library. He published his first novel in 1947 but then disappeared from the literary world for nearly two decades, working as a translator and publishing employee.
family_context_summary: Born to landless peasant parents in Azinhaga, Portugal. Family moved to Lisbon where father became a police officer. Extreme poverty; Saramago was transferred from grammar school to a technical school due to lack of money.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in literature or intellectual pursuits. Parents were rural laborers with minimal education.
evidence_summary: Saramago was born into extreme rural poverty in Portugal and received only a technical school education. He published a first novel at 25 that had no impact, and he himself concluded he 'didn't have anything worthwhile to say,' abandoning literary writing for 19 years. His literary fame came in his late 50s with 'Baltasar and Blimunda' (1982) and the Nobel Prize in 1998. The first novel was not a material milestone.

name: Johann Deisenhofer
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: By age 26 (Sep 1969), Deisenhofer was still a physics student at the Technical University of Munich, having started his studies in 1965 after military service. His PhD came in 1974 at age 31 and his Nobel Prize in 1988 at age 45. No material milestone by age 26 was found.
early_history_summary: Deisenhofer grew up on a family farm in Bavaria and was expected to take it over, but showed no interest in farming. His master's thesis in solid state physics introduced him to biophysics, and he pursued his PhD under Robert Huber at the Max Planck Institute.
family_context_summary: Born on a family farm in Zusamaltheim, Bavaria. Parents ran the farm; father returned from military service after WWII. Parents made the difficult decision to send him away to school when he showed no interest in farming.
parent_family_domain_summary: Farming family background; no scientific or academic domain connection. Parents supported education despite farm tradition.
evidence_summary: Deisenhofer came from a farming family in Bavaria and was expected to inherit the farm, but his parents supported his academic path. He began physics studies at 22 after military service and was still a student at 26. His PhD (1974) and Nobel Prize (1988) came much later. No material milestone by age 26 was identified.

name: Gerhard Richter
milestone_by_age_26: Received his diploma from the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts in 1956 at age 24 and became a master student with his own studio; subsequently received mural commissions that were well-received by officials and the public in East Germany by 1958.
early_history_summary: Richter grew up in Reichenau and Waltersdorf in Saxony under Nazism and then East German communism. He left school at 15 and apprenticed as an advertising and stage-set painter before being accepted to the Dresden Art Academy in 1951. He studied mural painting under Heinz Lohmar, received his diploma in 1956, and became a master student with a three-year studio. His successful Social Realist mural commissions allowed him to travel to the West, where he encountered avant-garde art at Documenta II in 1959.
primary_leverage_engine: Academy training and mural painting commissions
family_context_summary: Born in Dresden. Father was a mathematics and physics student who became a village teacher. Mother Hildegard was a bookseller's daughter with a passion for literature and music who encouraged Richter's interest in drawing and painting. Maternal grandfather was a gifted pianist.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother encouraged art and exposed Richter to literature and music from childhood. No direct art-world connections, but cultured family environment.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Dresden Academy, mural painting apprenticeship, cultured mother, East German constraints, master student studio
evidence_summary: Richter grew up in wartime and post-war East Germany with a cultured mother who encouraged his artistic interests. He apprenticed as a painter from age 17 and spent five years at the Dresden Art Academy, becoming a master student with his own studio at 24. His mural commissions were well-received, but the constraints of Socialist Realism and East Germany limited his artistic frontier. His most famous work came after his escape to the West in 1961, but the academy training and professional commissions by 26 were material career milestones.

name: Edsger W. Dijkstra
milestone_by_age_26: Created the shortest-path algorithm (Dijkstra's algorithm) in 1956 at age 26 for the inauguration of the ARMAC computer at the Mathematical Centre in Amsterdam — one of the most influential algorithms in computer science, published in 1959.
early_history_summary: Dijkstra was born in Rotterdam to a chemistry teacher father and a mathematically gifted mother who influenced his elegant approach to problem-solving. He scored the highest possible marks in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology on his school exams in 1948. He began studying theoretical physics at the University of Leyden but, after attending a programming course at Cambridge in 1951, was offered a part-time programming position at the Mathematical Centre in Amsterdam from 1952. By 1955 he chose programming over physics, and in 1956 devised his famous shortest-path algorithm.
primary_leverage_engine: Scarce skill in early computing and mathematical elegance
family_context_summary: Born in Rotterdam. Father was a high school chemistry teacher who was president of the Dutch Chemical Society but refused scientific promotion. Mother was a trained mathematician who never held a formal position but greatly influenced Dijkstra's mathematical thinking and emphasis on elegance.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a chemist with broad scientific knowledge; mother was a mathematician who shaped his approach to elegant problem-solving. Strong scientific household but not wealthy.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Mathematical mother, Cambridge programming course, van Wijngaarden mentorship, Mathematical Centre Amsterdam, early computer access, highest exam marks
evidence_summary: Dijkstra grew up in a scientifically rich household — his father was a chemist and his mother a mathematician who shaped his elegant problem-solving style. He scored perfect marks in science exams and was steered toward physics, but a 1951 Cambridge programming course led to a position at the Mathematical Centre in Amsterdam, one of the world's few computing centers. His mentor van Wijngaarden persuaded him that programming could become a respectable science. Access to early computers and four years of programming experience enabled him to create the shortest-path algorithm at 26, a foundational contribution to computer science.
